paper_title: SciGame: Let Agents Play the Scientific Discovery Games in the Real and Counterfactual World

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large language model agents are increasingly used for scientific discovery. However, existing benchmarks mix law inference with programming, score data fitting instead of prediction on unseen inputs, and do not separate empirical evidence from pretrained priors. We introduce SciGame, a controlled benchmark that converts scientific literature into structured scientific cards. Each card yields a pair of Original and dimensionally consistent Counterfactual environments with the same task interface. SciGame contains a Historical collection of canonical laws and a live Temporal collection curated from papers published after model knowledge cutoffs. It evaluates agents in candidate-guided Identification and open-ended Discovery settings. Each setting runs under Prior-only, Fixed, and Adaptive protocols. Experiments on five frontier models yield three findings. First, familiar priors hurt performance once the governing relation is altered. Second, adaptive experimentation helps the strongest models but harms weaker ones under limited budgets. Third, good explanations can hide quantitative failures. Recovering the exact symbolic form remains the main bottleneck, even when agents interpret evidence correctly. Current agents can investigate systems actively, but inducing exact laws in unfamiliar settings remains an open challenge.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Scientific discovery is sequential process in which researchers formulate hypotheses, design experiments, interpret observations, and draw conclusions under specified conditions. LLMs increasingly support this process. They analyze scientific descriptions (M. Bran et al., 2024; Laurent et al., 2024), construct executable expressions (Shojaee et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2024), interact with simulated environments (Wang et al., 2022), and propose experiments to test hypotheses (Boiko et al., 2023; 1 Scientific law discovery requires more than fitting data (Schmidt and Lipson, 2009; Brunton et al., 2016; Udrescu and Tegmark, 2020). An agent needs to infer how inputs determine observables and generalize to unqueried inputs (Kronberger et al., 2022). It needs to separate evidence from prior knowledge (Kronberger et al., 2022; RíosGarcía et al., 2026), revise hypotheses that contradict observations (Wilie et al., 2024; Jhaveri et al., 2026), and explain the relation and its applicability conditions. benchmark should therefore evaluate the whole investigation (Ríos-García et al., 2026). Existing benchmarks cover parts of this process. Some evaluate experiment selection and hypothesis revision interactively (Jansen et al., 2024; Bertolazzi et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2025a). Some recover equations from data (Shojaee et al., 2025) or link modeling with active experimental design (Gandhi et al., 2025; Kabra et al., 2026). Others test reasoning under altered physical laws (Koblischke et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025b; Zheng et al., 2026; Wiemann et al., 2026) or build tasks from publications (Majumder et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025c; Starace et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026a). Four gaps remain. First, benchmarks often change the task, observation protocol, and metric together. Few compare prior-only reasoning, fixed observations, and adaptive experimentation on one interface, or pair original and counterfactual relations (Chen et al., 2025b; Zheng et al., 2026; Wiemann et al., 2026). Second, common metrics may not test generalization to unseen inputs, and plausible explanation can score well even when the predictor is wrong (Ríos-García et al., 2026). Third, most benchmarks are static and rarely include relations published after models knowledge cutoff (White et al., 2025; He et al., 2026). Fourth, paper-based tasks mix law discovery with programming and replication (Kon et al., 2026). sections.content: We introduce SCIGAME, controlled benchmark for scientific law discovery by LLM agents. It converts source relations into scientific cards that record the relation, variables, input domains, and applicability conditions. Each card yields two environments with the same interface. The Original environment implements the source relation. The Counterfactual environment applies dimensionally consistent mutation. This pairing tests whether an agent follows evidence over familiar laws. In Identification, the agent selects the governing relation from candidates. In Discovery, no candidates are given. In both, the agent submits executable expressions, an explanation, and applicability conditions. Each task runs under three protocols. Under Prior-only, the agent receives no observations. Under Fixed, it receives observations from preset design. Under Adaptive, it queries an Oracle for experiments and decides when to submit. SCIGAME also includes live, knowledge-cutoffaware track. The Historical collection holds stable reference relations. The Temporal collection is built by rerunnable pipeline that extracts relations from recent papers and reviews them independently. Its time window moves with model cutoffs to reduce memorization (Rein et al., 2023; White et al., 2025). We report prediction score on hidden inputs, hierarchical episode success rate, and rubric-based explanation score (Zheng et al., 2023; Tan et al., 2025). Our contributions are as follows. First, we build controlled benchmark with paired Original and Counterfactual environments and two task settings. Second, we introduce live Temporal collection with an updatable curation pipeline. Third, we provide unified framework that compares three protocols with three metrics. Finally, we evaluate multiple LLMs and find that familiar priors help on Original relations but hurt on Counterfactual ones. Adaptive experimentation helps stronger models but can harm weaker ones. Wrong functional relations are the main failure mode, and good explanations can coexist with incorrect predictors. Code and data are available in this anonymous repository.

sections.title: 3.2 Data curation
sections.content: Scientific data sources. We compile two collections of source relations. The Historical collection contains relations from the history of science. These relations serve as interpretable references. They test whether agents can use established relations to make predictions and support their conclusions with evidence. The Temporal collection extracts relations from publications in configurable time window. We set this window after the reported knowledge cutoff of the evaluated Player 3 to reduce data contamination. Scientific data construction. For each task family, we create scientific card that records the relation, variables, input domains, and applicability conditions. Historical relations use fixed modeling assumptions with explicit controllable inputs and observables. Figure 2 shows the live curation pipeline for the Temporal collection. It keeps only papers whose journal publication date and first preprint date both fall after the knowledge cutoff of the evaluated Player. An LLM extracts quantitative relations from these papers. separate LLM reviewer checks each card for accuracy and completeness. Cards with missing or unsupported information are revised or removed. The pipeline can be rerun with new date windows to update the benchmark. Appendix lists all prompts. Counterfactual construction. For each task family in both collections, we pair an Original environment with Counterfactual environment. The Original environment uses the source relation. The Counterfactual environment uses systematically mutated version of it. Both environments share the same controllable inputs, input ranges, observables, and experimental constraints. They differ only in the relation that generates observations. This pairing tests whether the Player adapts to evidence that conflicts with established priors. Following NewtonBench (Zheng et al., 2026), we apply structural mutations to coefficients and exponents, add nonlinear transformations, and introduce cross-input interactions. Nonlinear transformations keep dimensional consistency, and each mutated variable is updated in all related equations. Appendix describes the mutation protocols for Historical and Temporal families. Finally, we evaluate the ground-truth equations of each environment on observations from its counterpart. All of them fail the prediction evaluation, which confirms that the two environments can be told apart empirically.

sections.title: 3.3 Experimental framework and protocol
sections.content: We define two task settings for each Original and Counterfactual environment. Identification. The Player receives formula that combines the Original and Counterfactual expressions through an unknown parameter s, Gr(x; s) = (1 s) gr(x) + r(x). (1) Setting = 0 gives the Original expression gr(x), 4 and = 1 gives the Counterfactual expression r(x). The task states whether intermediate values of are allowed. In that case, the formula interpolates linearly between the two predictions. The simulator always sets to zero or one, but this value is hidden from the Player. Discovery. The Player receives no candidate expressions or parametric models. It builds relation from inputs to observables using only the background description, experimental constraints, and available observations. Each scientific family therefore yields four tasks. Both settings require executable expressions for the observables and scientific explanation. Within an environment, they share the same experimental interface and numerical evaluation criteria. An episode is one run of the Player on one task under one protocol. Each episode starts with an empty interaction history and is isolated from other episodes. Figure 3 compares the three protocols. (1) Prior-only. The Player receives no observations and does not interact with the Oracle. It completes the task using only the task description, protocol instructions, and prior knowledge. (2) Fixed. The framework provides observations from prespecified design with fixed budget. The Player cannot select, modify, or repeat experiments. It then submits final completion in the same format as Prior-only. (3) Adaptive. The Player starts with no observations and proposes experiments to the Oracle step by step. At each LLM call, it receives the task description, protocol instructions, available observations, and interaction history. It returns structured response with at least two hypotheses and their confidence scores, which are nonnegative and sum to one. The response also contains either an experimental proposal or final completion. Each proposal includes numerical prediction under every hypothesis for each proposed input and requested observable. Each final completion includes predictor, scientific rationale, and its applicability conditions. The Oracle checks each proposal against the experimental constraints. It returns simulated observations for an accepted proposal. For rejected proposal, it returns constraint feedback without any observations. The framework appends the proposal and the response to the interaction history. The Figure 2: Data curation pipeline. sections.title: 4.2 Main benchmark results
sections.content: Overall performance. Table 2 reports the episode success rate (ESR) and average prediction score (PS) of five Players under the Prior-only, Fixed with = 4, and Adaptive protocols. We summarize four findings. (1) Rooted priors act as burden when learning counterfactual laws. In Original Discovery under Fixed, the average ESR is 58.6% on Historical tasks and 21.3% on Temporal tasks across all nine LLMs. This pattern reverses in Counterfactual Discovery. On Historical counterfactuals, strict ESR drops to zero for all LLMs. On Temporal counterfactuals, the average reaches 8.9%. Under Adaptive, the top model also scores 16.7% on Temporal counterfactuals and 1.7% on Historical ones. This reversal suggests that familiar priors may keep LLMs from accepting counterfactual relations. (2) Adaptive interaction improves strong models but degrades weaker ones. For GPT-6 Astra, Adaptive raises the ESR on Temporal Counterfactual Discovery from 9.7% to 16.7%; for Qwen3.7 Plus and GPT-5.6 Terra, it stays flat or drops, from 6.9% to 6.9% and from 8.3% to 1.4%, respectively. On Temporal Original Discovery, GPT-5.6 Terra drops from 20.8% to 6.9% and Qwen3.7 Plus from 13.9% to 6.9%. Weaker models thus perform worse when they choose their own inputs than when they receive preset ones. (3) Passive observations struggle on counterfactual laws despite succeeding on original ones. sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Our experiments cover small set of models, mostly from the GPT family, run through one agent harness. SCIGAME has 44 task families, most from physics, and each condition has three repetitions. Small differences between cells are therefore uncertain. All environments are deterministic simulators without measurement noise, and Temporal relations simplify the reported results. Counterfactual relations come from limited set of synthetic mutations, and the two collections use different mutation schemes. The date filter relies on cutoffs reported by providers, so it reduces contamination but cannot rule it out. Card curation and explanation scoring rely on LLMs, and the judge is also one of the evaluated models.

sections.title: A Details of benchmark implementation
sections.content: This appendix specifies the Adaptive interaction protocol and the evalution pipeline. A.1 Adaptive interaction protocol Figure 8 illustrates the interaction loop under the Adaptive protocol. In each step, the Player submits structured report bundling its current hypotheses, corresponding confidence scores, and an experimental proposal with prior expectation results. Upon receiving feedback from the Oracle, the Player either revises its hypotheses to design subsequent experiments or terminates the episode by submitting final predictor under the stopping rule described below. Figure 8: Adaptive interaction mechanism between the Player and the Oracle. Report schema and hypothesis tracking. Each hypothesis consists of scientific statement and reported confidence score in [0, 1]. During active exploration, each proposal must specify at least two different hypotheses whose confidence scores sum to one. Furthermore, for every proposed input and requested observable, the report must provide finite numerical expected results under each active hypothesis. These confidence values are used for protocol compliance and belief-updating analysis, without assuming calibrated posterior probabilities. For the final completion (across Prior-only, Fixed, and Adaptive protocols), the submission must designate selected hypothesis with an executable predictor ˆg, scientific explanation, and explicit applicability conditions. Table 3 summarizes the data schema across all interaction stages. Oracle validation and stopping criterion. Before executing any proposal, the Oracle validates the requested apparatus, input domains, observables, 12 and experimental constraints. Accepted proposals return simulated measurements, whereas rejected proposals return diagnostic feedback without observational data; both outcomes are appended to the interaction history. Under the Adaptive protocol, the Player may request another experiment only while every reported hypothesis confidence remains strictly below the task threshold τ . Conversely, valid final submission must select hypothesis with confidence at least τ . Crucially, protocol compliance is evaluated independently of predictive accuracy: submission violating the stopping rule can still be evaluated for its continuous prediction score (see in Figure 4), but the episode is automatically marked as failure under the episode success rate (ESR). Deterministic numerical observations. For an accepted proposal at step t, let xt be the input vector and At the set of requested observable indices. The Oracle returns deterministic observations yt,r defined as: yt,r = Qr(gr(xt)) , At, (3) where gr() is the ground-truth response function and Qr quantizes the simulator response to the declared measurement resolution of observable r. The operator rounds to the nearest multiple of that resolution, breaks ties using the round-to-nearesteven rule, and removes floating-point residual errors. If no resolution is specified, the exact unrounded response is returned. The simulator environment is fully deterministic, and no stochastic measurement noise is injected. sections.title: B Addtional experimental results
sections.content: Success episode distribution of Adaptive on Temporal collection. Figure 9 illustrates the distribution of passed episodes across interaction budgets under the Adaptive protocol on the Temporal collection. In both Original and Counterfactual Identification, successful episodes are overwhelmingly concentrated at budget one across all evaluated models, confirming that single targeted query suffices to discriminate between candidate relations. Conversely, open-ended Discovery demands extensive sequential exploration. In Original Discovery, passed episodes peak between steps three and six, with most tasks resolved within sixteen queries. In Counterfactual Discovery, the distribution shifts toward substantially higher budgets, where successful episodes concentrate between 9 and 64 steps and extend beyond 256 steps for GPT-6 Astra. This distribution directly accounts for the cold start observed in Adaptive discovery, demonstrating that overturning familiar priors to infer counterfactual functional forms requires much larger interaction budget than static evaluation. Inference cost of the main benchmark. Does more inference lead to better discovery? In Table 6, Figure 10 reports the cost of the main matrix by the Player and method. The total is $5,843. Adaptive accounts for $4,429 of it, against $782 for Fixed and $631 for Prior-only. Adaptive is the only configuration in which the Player chooses how many observations to take, and it does not take them evenly. Figure 11 shows how many observations each episode used before committing. Most episodes stop after one or two, while small number run far longer and one GPT-6-Astra episode reaches 485. Those long episodes are the ones that fail. Successful episodes stop after 1.3 to 2.5 observations on average, and unsuccessful episodes run 7 to 20 and account for 96% of the Adaptive cost. The extra budget is spent searching rather than solving. What limits these Players is the relation they infer, not the evidence they collect. Weak and strict ESR results. Table 7 shows models consistently achieve higher weak ESR than strict ESR. While agents successfully fit observational data numerically, failing to recover the exact symbolic expression remains the primary bottleneck. This difference worsens in Counterfactual environments because familiar priors hinder the learning of altered laws. In Historical Counterfactual Discovery, strict ESR drops to 0.0% for most models, and GPT-6 Astra reaches only 1.7% despite 95.0% weak ESR. Performance is also lower on the Temporal collection, peaking at 16.7% strict ESR in Counterfactual Discovery. These results confirm that inducing exact symbolic equations in unfamiliar settings remains an challenge in this paradigm.
